Abstract.

This paper investigates a high-dimensional chemotaxis system with consumption of chemoattractant

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v),vt=Δ​v−u​v,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv,\\ \end{array}\right.

under homogeneous boundary conditions of Neumann type, in a bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥4)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}~(n\geq 4) with smooth boundary. It is proved that if initial data satisfy u0∈C0​(Ω¯)u_{0}\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}) and v0∈W1,q​(Ω)v_{0}\in W^{1,q}(\Omega) for some q>nq>n, the model possesses at least one global renormalized solution.

Key words and phrases: 
Keller-Segel model; Renormalized solutions; Entropy method; Global existence
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
35A01, 35K57, 35Q92, 92C17.

1. Introduction

In this paper, we consider the global existence of renormalized solutions to the chemotaxis system with consumption of chemoattractant

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−u​v,x∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,&{}x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),~v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),&{}x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

in a bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥4)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}~(n\geq 4) with smooth boundary, where the scalar functions u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) denote bacterial density and the oxygen concentration, respectively. u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are given functions. ∂∂ν\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu} denotes the differentiation with respect to the outward normal derivative on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Model (1) was initially introduced by Keller and Segel [11] to describe the traveling band behavior of chemotactic bacteria, that is, the biased movement of bacteria to the oxygen concentration gradient. It can be regarded as the ‘fluid-free’ version of the coupled chemotaxis-fluid model which was first presented in [17]. Aerobic bacteria such as Bacillus subtilis often live in thin fluid layers near solid-air-water contact line, in which the biology of chemotaxis, metabolism, and cell-cell signaling is intimately connected to the physics of buoyancy, diffusion, and mixing [17].

In the last few years, model (1) has been studied by some authors. It has been shown by Tao [15] that (1) admits global classical bounded solutions under the assumption that n≥2n\geq 2 and ‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} be sufficiently small. In [16], Tao and Winkler proved that if n=2n=2, (1) possesses a unique global classical solution which is bounded and satisfies u⁡(x,t)→u¯0:=1|Ω|​∫Ωu0u(x,t)\rightarrow\bar{u}_{0}:=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u_{0} and v⁡(x,t)→0v(x,t)\rightarrow 0 as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty; in the case n=3n=3, for arbitrary large initial data, this problem possesses at least one global weak solution which becomes eventually smooth and also satisfies (u,v)→(u¯0,0)(u,v)\rightarrow(\bar{u}_{0},0) as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. Furthermore, Zhang and Li [24] obtained that if either n≤2n\leq 2 or ‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)≤16​(n+1),n≥3\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\frac{1}{6(n+1)},n\geq 3, the global classical solution of (1) converges to (u¯0,0)(\bar{u}_{0},0) exponentially in the large time limit. Similarly, the chemotaxis fluid system has been investigated by some authors, we refer to [7, 13, 20, 14, 21, 23] for the further reading.

The concept of renormalized solutions was introduced by Diperna and Lions [4, 5, 6]. In [8], Fischer established the global existence of renormalized solutions to reaction-diffusion systems with entropy-dissipating reactions. Chen and Jüngel [3] proved the global-in-time existence of renormalized solutions to reaction-cross-diffusion systems for an arbitrary number of variables in bounded domains with no-flux boundary conditions. For the global existence of renormalized solutions of the Landau equation and Boltzmann equation, see for example [1, 2, 18]. Recently, it was shown in [22] that the Keller-Segel system with singular sensitivity and signal absorption admits renormalized radial solutions (u,v)(u,v) which are continuous in (Ω¯∖{0})×[0,∞)(\overline{\Omega}\setminus\{0\})\times[0,\infty) and smooth in (Ω¯∖{0})×(0,∞)(\overline{\Omega}\setminus\{0\})\times(0,\infty), and which solve the corresponding initial-boundary value problem in an appropriate generalized sense.

To the best of our knowledge, for arbitrarily large initial data, whether any kind of solution to (1) in high-dimensional exists globally has been an open problem. The difficulty mainly arises from the cross-diffusive term in the first equation when considering the global existence of weak solutions. The known energy estimates are not sufficient to guarantee the boundedness of u∇vu\nabla v in Ls​(Ω×[0,T])​(s>1)L^{s}(\Omega\times[0,T])(s>1). Therefore, we consider renormalized solutions.

Main results. As usual, we shall assume that the initial data u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} satisfy

{u0∈C0(Ω¯),u0>0inΩ¯,v0∈W1,q​(Ω)for​some​q>n,v0>0​in​Ω¯.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{0}\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}),\ \ \ u_{0}>0\ \mathrm{in}\ \overline{\Omega},\\ v_{0}\in W^{1,q}(\Omega)\ \ \ \mathrm{for\ some}\ q>n,\ v_{0}>0\ \mathrm{in}\ \overline{\Omega}.\end{array}\right.

Our main result reads as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝn,n≥4\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n},n\geq 4 be a bounded convex domain with smooth boundary, and suppose that u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} satisfy (1). Then there exists a global renormalized solution of (1) in the sense of Definition 5.1 below.

In order to construct renormalized solutions, we use the notation from [8]. Let φE:ℝ0+→ℝ0+,E∈ℕ\varphi_{E}:\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+},E\in\mathbb{N}, be truncation function subject to the following conditions:
(E1) Let φE∈C2​(ℝ0+)\varphi_{E}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}).
(E2) Assume that there exists K1>0K_{1}>0 so that v​|φE′′​(v)|≤K1v|\varphi_{E}^{\prime\prime}(v)|\leq K_{1} holds for all EE and all v∈ℝ0+v\in\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}.
(E3) Suppose that for every EE the set suppD​φED\varphi_{E} is bounded.
(E4) Assume that limE→∞φE′​(v)=1\lim_{E\rightarrow\infty}\varphi_{E}^{\prime}(v)=1 holds for all v∈ℝ0+v\in\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}.
(E5) Suppose that there exists K2>0K_{2}>0 such that |φE′​(v)|≤K2|\varphi_{E}^{\prime}(v)|\leq K_{2} holds for every v∈ℝ0+v\in\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+} and every EE.
(E6) Assume that φE​(v)=v\varphi_{E}(v)=v holds for any v∈ℝ0+v\in\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+} with v<Ev<E.
(E7) Suppose that we have limE→∞sup|v|≤K|φE′′​(v)|=0\lim_{E\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{|v|\leq K}|\varphi_{E}^{\prime\prime}(v)|=0 for every K∈ℝ+K\in\mathbb{R}^{+}.

Such truncations φE\varphi_{E} satisfying (E1)-(E7) can indeed be constructed. Let ϕ∈C∞​(ℝ)\phi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) be a smooth nonincreasing function taking values in [0,1][0,1] with ϕ≡1\phi\equiv 1 for x<0x<0 and ϕ≡0\phi\equiv 0 for x>1x>1. Define

(1.9) φE​(v):=v​ϕ​(v−EE)+3​E​(1−ϕ⁡(v−EE)).\varphi_{E}(v):=v\phi\left(\frac{v-E}{E}\right)+3E\left(1-\phi\bigg(\frac{v-E}{E}\bigg)\right).

Then one verifies readily that φE\varphi_{E} satisfy conditions (E1)-(E7). Note that we shall also use the same family of truncations in the construction of our renormalized solutions below.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce a family of regularized problems and give some preliminary properties. Based on an energy-type inequality, a priori estimates are given in Section 3. Section 4 is devoted to showing the global existence of the regularized problems. Finally, we give the proof of the main result in Section 5.

2. Approximate problems

According to the idea from [16], we consider the approximate problems

{uε​t=Δuε−∇⋅(uεFε′(uε)∇vε),x∈Ω,t>0,vε​t=Δ​vε−Fε​(uε)​vε,x∈Ω,t>0,∂uε∂ν=∂vε∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,uε(x,0)=u0(x),vε(x,0)=v0(x),x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{\varepsilon t}=\Delta u_{\varepsilon}-\nabla\cdot(u_{\varepsilon}F_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})\nabla v_{\varepsilon}),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ v_{\varepsilon t}=\Delta v_{\varepsilon}-F_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})v_{\varepsilon},&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \frac{\partial u_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=0,&{}x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0,\\ u_{\varepsilon}(x,0)=u_{0}(x),~v_{\varepsilon}(x,0)=v_{0}(x),&{}x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1).

The approximate function Fε{F_{\varepsilon}} in (2) can be chosen as

Fε​(s):=1ε​ln⁡(1+ε​s),for​all​s≥0.\displaystyle{F_{\varepsilon}}(s):=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\ln(1+\varepsilon s),\ \ \mathrm{for\ all}\ s\geq 0.

Note that our choice of Fε{F_{\varepsilon}} ensures that

(2.6) 0≤Fε′​(s)=11+ε​s≤1,and​ 0≤Fε​(s)≤sfor​all​s≥0,0\leq{F_{\varepsilon}}^{\prime}(s)=\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon s}\leq 1,\ \ \mathrm{and}\ \ 0\leq{F_{\varepsilon}}(s)\leq s\ \ \mathrm{for\ all}\ s\geq 0,
(2.7) s​Fε′​(s)=s1+ε​s≤1ε,for​all​s≥0,s{F_{\varepsilon}}^{\prime}(s)=\frac{s}{1+\varepsilon s}\leq\frac{1}{\varepsilon},\ \ \mathrm{for\ all}\ s\geq 0,

and that

(2.8) Fε′​(s)↗1andFε​(s)↗sas​ε↘0for​all​s≥0.{F_{\varepsilon}}^{\prime}(s)\nearrow 1\ \ \mathrm{and}\ \ {F_{\varepsilon}}(s)\nearrow s\ \ \mathrm{as}\ \varepsilon\searrow 0\ \ \mathrm{for\ all}\ s\geq 0.

All the above approximate problems admit local-in-time smooth solutions:

Lemma 2.1.

Suppose that u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} satisfy (1), then for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there exist Tm​a​x,ε∈(0,∞]T_{max,\varepsilon}\in(0,\infty] and a classical solution (uε,vε)(u_{\varepsilon},v_{\varepsilon}) of (2) in Ω×(0,Tm​a​x,ε)\Omega\times(0,T_{max,\varepsilon}). Moreover, if Tm​a​x,ε<∞T_{max,\varepsilon}<\infty, then

(2.9) ‖uε​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖vε​(⋅,t)‖W1,q​(Ω)→∞,as​t↗Tm​a​x,ε.\|{u_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|{v_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,q}(\Omega)}\rightarrow\infty,\ \mathrm{as}~t\nearrow T_{max,\varepsilon}.

The proof of this lemma is based on well-established methods involving the Banach fixed point theorem, the standard regularity theories of parabolic equations (see [20] for instance).

The following estimates of uε{u_{\varepsilon}} and vε{v_{\varepsilon}} are basic but important in the proof of our result.

Lemma 2.2.

For each ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), we have

(2.10) ∫Ωuε​(⋅,t)=∫Ωu0for​all​t∈(0,Tm​a​x,ε)\int_{\Omega}{u_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,t)=\int_{\Omega}u_{0}\ \ \ \mathrm{for\ all}\ t\in(0,T_{max,\varepsilon})

and

(2.11) ‖vε​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)in​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x,ε).\|{v_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\ \ \ \mathrm{in}\ \Omega\times(0,T_{max,\varepsilon}).
Proof.

Integrating the first equation in (2), we obtain (2.10). And an application of the maximum principle to the second equation in (2) gives (2.11). ∎

3. A priori estimates

This section is devoted to establishing an energy-type inequality which will play a key role in the derivation of further estimates.

Lemma 3.1.

For each ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), the solution of (2) satisfies

(3.1) dd​t​{∫Ωuε​ln⁡uε+2​∫Ω|∇vε|2}+∫Ω|∇uε|2uε+∫Ωvε​|D2​ln⁡vε|2+12​∫ΩFε​(uε)​|∇vε|2vε≤0\frac{d}{dt}\left\{\int_{\Omega}u_{\varepsilon}\ln u_{\varepsilon}+2\int_{\Omega}|\nabla\sqrt{v_{\varepsilon}}|^{2}\right\}+\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}}{u_{\varepsilon}}+\int_{\Omega}v_{\varepsilon}|D^{2}\ln v_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}F_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})\frac{|\nabla v_{\varepsilon}|^{2}}{v_{\varepsilon}}\leq 0

for all t∈(0,Tm​a​x,ε)t\in(0,T_{max,\varepsilon}).

Proof.

The proof is based on the first two equations in (2) and integration by parts, we refer readers to [20, Lemmas 3.1-3.4] for details. ∎

We next collect some consequences of the above energy inequality which are convenient for our purpose.

5. Existence of renormalized solutions

Having established the existence of solutions for our approximate problem, we turn to the proof of the existence of renormalized solutions to the original equations (1). Before going into detail, let us first give the definition of renormalized solutions.

Definition 5.1.

Suppose that n≥1n\geq 1, that Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a bounded domain and that u0∈L1​(Ω)u_{0}\in L^{1}(\Omega) and v0∈L1​(Ω)v_{0}\in L^{1}(\Omega) are nonnegative. Then a pair (u,v)(u,v) of functions

u∈Lloc1​(Ω¯×[0,∞)),\displaystyle u\in L_{\rm{loc}}^{1}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)),
v∈Lloc∞​(Ω¯×[0,∞)),\displaystyle v\in L_{\rm{loc}}^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)),

lim supE→∞|μE|(Ω¯×[0,T))\displaystyle\limsup_{E\rightarrow\infty}|\mu^{E}|(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T)) ≤C∑K=1∞limε→0νεK(Ω¯×[0,T))limE→∞sup|v|∈[K−1,K)v|φE′′(v)|\displaystyle\leq C\sum_{K=1}^{\infty}\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\nu_{\varepsilon}^{K}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T))\lim_{E\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{|v|\in[K-1,K)}v|\varphi_{E}^{\prime\prime}(v)|
+C∑K=1∞limε→0γεK(Ω¯×[0,T))limE→∞sup|v|∈[K−1,K)v|φE′′(v)|\displaystyle\quad+C\sum_{K=1}^{\infty}\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\gamma_{\varepsilon}^{K}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T))\lim_{E\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{|v|\in[K-1,K)}v|\varphi_{E}^{\prime\prime}(v)|
=0.\displaystyle=0.

This finishes the proof of the lemma. ∎

We can now prove our main result.
